Square Biz
SKWAIR BIZ
noun (Boomer slang)
Shortened from square business, African-American slang of the 1960s–70s for the honest truth, serious matters, or straight dealing ("I’m telling you square business"), from square in its old sense of fair, honest, exact (a square deal, fair and square; Webster 1828: "That does equal justice; exact; fair; honest; as square dealing"). Teena Marie’s funk hit "Square Biz" (1981) made the short form famous.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Square biz means straight talk and honest dealing — "no jive, this is square business." It uses square not in the hippie sense of "uncool" but in the older sense of fair and true, the sense in a square deal and fair and square. The Christian observation: the phrase lands on one of the most practical virtues in Scripture — honesty in business. God cares about the scale in the marketplace: "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight" (Pro 11:1). "Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt" (Lev 19:36) — honesty in trade is grounded in redemption. The man who may dwell in God’s holy hill is "He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart" (Psa 15:2). Paul handled money for the churches carefully: "Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men" (2Co 8:21). In a culture of hustles, scams, and spin, a Christian whose word is square business is a witness. A father in business can teach his son that the square deal is not a weakness but a confession of faith in the God who sees the scales.

Webster 1828 Definition

1960s–70s AAVE slang (square business; Teena Marie, 1981) for honest truth and straight dealing — on the 1828 square, "honest, fair" — the just weight that is the LORD’s delight (Pro 11:1).

expand to see more

SQUARE BIZ, n. (AAVE, 1960s–70s; Boomer era) Honest truth; serious, legitimate business; straight dealing. From square business. "That’s square biz."

Webster (1828) — SQUARE, adjective 5. That does equal justice; exact; fair; honest; as square dealing.

Note the two Boomer squares: the hippie’s square (conventional, uncool — see Square) and the street’s square biz (honest). The second is the older and better one.

Modern Corruption

A wholesome phrase prizing honesty; Scripture grounds the square deal in the God who delights in a just weight and redeemed His people to live honestly.

expand to see more

Square biz needs no correction; it names a virtue. Its value is the contrast it draws with its own neighborhood of slang — jive, hustle, con, game — all words for dishonest talk and dealing. A community that has been cheated prizes a word for the honest man, and Scripture prizes him too.

The deeper point is that Scripture roots business honesty in theology. Lev 19:36 ties just weights to the Exodus: the God who freed you from Egypt’s cheating masters will not have you cheat your neighbors. A Christian businessman who keeps square accounts is not merely being prudent; he is confessing that he serves a God who sees every scale.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin exquadrare (to make square) → Old French esquare → English square (exact; honest, fair) + business → 1960s–70s AAVE square business → 1981 "Square Biz."

English square — true, exact; honest, fair (a square deal, fair and square)

1960s–70s AAVE: square business — the honest truth; legitimate dealing

1981: Teena Marie, "Square Biz"

Hebrew eben shelemah — "a just weight," literally a whole stone (Pro 11:1)
